### Question 1

Count them on your fingers: what the studies show, what the clinician knows about this patient, and what the patient wants. Three inputs, and the decision needs all three because each answers a different question. The studies answer 'what works on average,' expertise answers 'does this apply to the person in front of me,' and preferences answer 'is this something the person will actually accept and continue.' Miss any one and you can still make a decision, but it stops being EBP.

### Question 2

Fifty-five percent delivered means forty-five percent missed — subtract from 100 and the leftover is the problem. The important part is what that leftover is made of: not exotic treatments, but ordinary care that everyone already agrees works and that simply did not happen. That is why EBP is framed as a delivery problem rather than a discovery problem. The knowledge exists; the job is getting it used consistently.

### Question 3

Clinical expertise is not the same thing as seniority or habit. Expertise means judgment built from assessing patients and reasoning about their responses; a schedule inherited from whoever set it up years ago carries none of that. So the honest count here is zero of three. The useful response is not to argue about the dressing, but to turn the discomfort into a question you can actually look up, which is the first thing EBP asks you to do.

### Question 4

The two activities point opposite ways along the same pipeline. Research adds to the pool of knowledge; EBP draws from it. A quick test for any project: ask whether it would still be worth doing if the answer were already published. If yes, it is EBP, because the point is to find and use that answer. If the whole purpose is that no one has the answer yet, it is research.

### Question 5

Eighteen out of 24 reduces to 3 out of 4, so 75 percent. Read the denominator carefully before you interpret anything: 6 out of 24 would be the nurses who did not report the barrier, and quoting that number would reverse the meaning of the survey. Once the proportion is right, the finding does real work, because a barrier reported by three quarters of a staff is a scheduling problem to be solved, not an attitude problem to be lectured about.

### Question 6

Add 17 to 2008 and you land on 2025 — long enough for a student who started nursing school when the paper came out to become an experienced charge nurse before the finding is routine. The number is worth remembering because it identifies where the bottleneck sits. Publishing is fast; adopting is slow. EBP programs target the slow part, which is why they focus on mentors, policies, and access rather than on producing more studies.

### Question 7

Forty-two out of 50 is the same as 84 out of 100, so 84 percent. Notice what the staff are describing: not a lack of interest, but a lack of the conditions that make looking things up possible during a shift. That is why the fixes that work are structural. A mentor supplies the appraisal skill, protected time supplies the minutes, and a database at the bedside supplies the access, and the more of those three a unit puts in place, the more likely the behavior is to stick.

### Question 8

Two of three sounds like a win until you remember that the components are not votes to be counted; they are conditions that all have to be met. A plan the patient refuses has an effectiveness of zero no matter how strong the trial data are. So the useful move is to find out what the objection actually is, because it often points to an alternative that satisfies the evidence and the patient at the same time.

### Question 9

Retrieving 12 articles tells you only that 12 documents matched your search terms. Appraisal is where you ask three separate questions of each one: is it done well, does it answer my question, and does it apply to my patients. Skipping ahead to writing policy means the weakest article in the pile carries the same weight as the strongest, which defeats the purpose of searching in the first place.

### Question 10

Percent change always divides the size of the drop by where you started, so it is 3 divided by 8, not 3 divided by 5 and not 3 out of 100. Three-eighths is 0.375, or 37.5 percent. Also notice the second half of the answer: finding an improvement is not the end of EBP. You keep watching, because one unit measured once cannot separate the bundle's effect from everything else that changed at the same time.

### Question 11

Forty protocols with 26 backed by current evidence leaves 14 without, and 14 out of 40 is 35 percent — the count and the percentage are different numbers, so never report one in place of the other. The strategic point is what the audit is for. No unit can review 40 protocols at once, so you count the shaky ones, rank them, and spend the review time there instead of guessing which policy has quietly gone out of date.

### Question 12

Count what you actually have rather than what you wish you had: one guideline plus two small studies is three sources, not zero. "Best available" is doing real work in the definition of EBP, because rare problems will never accumulate large trials, and refusing to act until they do is itself a decision with consequences for the patient. So you use what exists, say plainly how confident it lets you be, involve the patient in that uncertainty, and then watch the outcomes closely enough to catch it if you were wrong.
